title: The golden lid
hookLine: the face of truth is hidden by a golden disc; uncover it (Isha Upanishad 15)
tomorrow: a monk crossing a desert kept saying one short text. which one?

cards: Gold foil on a chocolate box. A glossy ad at one in the morning. A phone screen so bright you can't see past the shine to what's on it.

The Isha Upanishad, near its end, names the thing hiding the truth, and it's gold. The face of truth is covered with a golden disc, it says. O Pushan, nourishing sun, uncover it, so that I, who love the truth, may see.
The gold is the sun's own glare. The same lines also appear in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, as a prayer at the end of a life.

teach.b: The Katha Upanishad tells a story about that lid. A boy named Nachiketa ends up at the door of Yama, the lord of death, and Yama grants him three wishes. For the third, Nachiketa asks: what happens after a person dies?
Yama tries to talk him out of it. Ask for sons and grandsons who live a hundred years. Ask for cattle, horses, gold, a kingdom, a long life.
Chariots, music, pleasures no one else could have. Nachiketa says: these last till tomorrow.

teach.h: KEEP YOUR HORSES AND YOUR SONGS.
teach.b: Keep your horses, keep your dancing and songs. Tell me the thing I asked. Then Yama gives the teaching behind the test.
There is the good, shreyas, and there is the pleasant, preyas. Both tie a person down. The wise choose the good; the foolish choose the pleasant.
Set beside the Isha, that's one way to hear the golden lid. The pleasant isn't evil; it's gold. It just sits right on top of the truth, shining.
And the Isha's verse doesn't ask to have the gold thrown away.
It asks the sun itself to pull back its rays: uncover it. The next verse goes further: the light that is your fairest form, I see it. Behind the glare isn't darkness.

how: Hindus recite the Isha's closing verses, including 'the face of truth is covered with a golden disc', and they appear as a prayer for the dying in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad; the Katha's teaching of the good and the pleasant is studied alongside them.

o: a bright, pleasing covering that hides what's true
the sun's disc, hiding nothing at all
a crown worn by the lord of death in the Katha

games.q: the boy, the lord of death, the lid: tap the pairs.
p: offered gold, horses and long life

s: in the Isha, the golden lid is something ugly hiding the truth
it's gold: the sun's own bright disc. the pleasant covers the good by shining, not by being ugly.
Nachiketa turns down horses, gold and long life to hear Yama's answer
in the Katha he says these last till tomorrow: keep them, and tell me what I asked.
the Isha's prayer asks for the sun to be put out
it asks Pushan to draw back his rays, so the speaker can see the fairest form of his light.

games.q: two job offers: one flashy, with a big title and photos for your feed; one plainer, closer to what you care about. Yama's teaching, what's the question to ask?
o: which is the good, shreyas, and which is just the pleasant, preyas?
which one shines brighter? the Isha says gold is where truth shows.
neither: the Katha says turn down every good thing that's offered.
games.why: Yama says both tie a person down, and the wise choose the good. the pleasant isn't evil; it just sits on top, shining.

practice: Find one shiny thing near you: a ring, a coin, a spoon, a phone screen. Tilt it until it catches the light and let yourself enjoy the glint for a moment.
Then hold it still and look past the shine to the thing itself, its shape, its weight, what it's actually for.

wordCard.voice: The golden lid: the Isha's picture of a bright covering over the face of truth, and the prayer to the sun to lift it.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Isha Upanishad 15: by a golden vessel the face of truth is covered.

carryVoice: Here's the line: uncover it, past the glint to the good. That's the Isha, all four days of it.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 15–16 (the face of truth covered by a golden disc; O Pushan, uncover it; the fairest form of your light I see)
Katha Upanishad 1.1.20–29 (Nachiketa's third wish; Yama's offers; 'these last till tomorrow; keep your horses, dance and song')
Katha Upanishad 1.2.1–2 (the good, shreyas, and the pleasant, preyas)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.15 (the same verses as a prayer at death)
